title: Fed's Warsh Says Staff Are Sketching Out AI Contingencies
summary: Opening the San Francisco Fed's Productivity and Jobs Task Force, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh calls super intelligence the most transformative force of his lifetime and argues, drawing on growth theory, that it could automate the very process of generating new ideas, while insisting humans must remain the ones making final decisions. He says the Fed will neither cheer nor resist the technology but will plan for it, and he lays out three staff scenarios that he stresses are illustrations rather than forecasts. In the first the gains are widely shared and employment stays strong, in the second growth is fast but workers are displaced and unemployment rises, and in the third AI disappoints, valuations fall and the economy slows before recovering without the hoped-for productivity boost.
focus: Shadow the passage where Warsh walks through the three staff scenarios one by one, since each follows the same clear structure of growth, jobs and outcome, and then his short explanation of why the Fed is doing contingency planning rather than forecasting, which is ideal practice for measured, hedged policy language.

vocab.meaning: lasting only a very short time
vocab.context: Warsh said the new task forces are meant to look beyond short-lived monthly data points and focus on deeper trends.
vocab.example: We should not reprice the whole portfolio on the back of a fleeting dip in one quarter's demand.

vocab.meaning: a particular combination of events or circumstances, especially a critical moment
vocab.context: He described the present as a pivotal moment in which the economy and technology are changing at the same time.
vocab.example: At this conjuncture of rising rates and slowing demand, the board needs a clear view on which units to fund.

vocab.meaning: simplified to show only the main features, not every real detail
vocab.context: Warsh described the economic models he drew on as simplified frameworks that capture the big picture.
vocab.example: This is a stylized cost curve, so treat the numbers as directional rather than precise.

vocab.meaning: coming from inside a system rather than from outside it
vocab.context: He referred to the school of growth theory in which new ideas, produced within the economy, drive long-run prosperity.
vocab.example: The client's margin squeeze is largely endogenous, driven by its own pricing decisions rather than the market.

vocab.meaning: able to be used by many people at once without being used up
vocab.zh: 非竞争性的（可同时被多人使用）
vocab.context: Warsh explained that ideas are expensive to discover but, once found, can be shared by everyone at almost no cost.
vocab.example: Because software is nonrival, the marginal cost of serving one more customer is close to zero.

vocab.meaning: to gradually become smaller or weaker
vocab.context: One of his open questions was when the productivity gains from AI might start to fade.
vocab.example: We expect cost savings to taper after year two, once the easy automation wins are captured.

vocab.meaning: fair and not favouring any side
vocab.context: Warsh joked that he is not entirely neutral, admitting he wants America to lead in the technology.
vocab.example: We brought in an impartial third party to run the vendor evaluation so no business unit could steer it.

vocab.meaning: modest; not claiming to be very important
vocab.context: He called the Fed's role a modest one, focused on asking the right questions rather than predicting the future.
vocab.example: Our ask is humble: a three-month pilot in one region before any wider rollout.

vocab.meaning: a possible future event that you prepare for in case it happens
vocab.context: Warsh said Fed staff are preparing for several possible AI outcomes instead of betting on one forecast.
vocab.example: The integration plan includes a contingency for losing key engineers in the first six months.

vocab.meaning: the person who makes the final decision
vocab.context: He stressed that however capable the technology becomes, people must remain the ones who make the final calls.
vocab.example: The steering committee can advise, but the CFO is the decider on capital allocation.

vocab.meaning: a long-lasting period of weak economic growth, not caused by the normal business cycle
vocab.context: Warsh mentioned the long-running worry that growth has slowed because good ideas are becoming harder to find.
vocab.example: If the sector is in secular stagnation, cost cutting alone will not restore the growth story investors want.

vocab.meaning: a technology that spreads across the whole economy and changes many industries, like electricity
vocab.context: He compared super intelligence to earlier breakthroughs such as electricity and the engine that transformed every sector.
vocab.example: Treat generative AI as a general-purpose technology, so the question is not whether to adopt it but where first.

vocab.meaning: the part of output growth not explained by more labour or capital, often seen as a measure of innovation and efficiency
vocab.context: Warsh listed how AI might change this measure of efficiency as one of the key questions for the task force.
vocab.example: The plant added headcount and machines, but total factor productivity barely moved, so the process itself is the problem.

phrases.meaning: a check made suddenly, without warning
phrases.context: Warsh opened with a joke that his first visit to a regional Reserve Bank as chair was a surprise inspection.
phrases.example: The new COO likes to do snap inspections of the warehouses rather than rely on monthly reports.

phrases.meaning: an activity that only succeeds when people work together
phrases.context: He thanked the organisers and described central banking as something no one can do alone.
phrases.example: Post-merger integration is a team sport, so we need finance, HR and IT in the room from day one.

phrases.meaning: good enough and suitable for the job it is meant to do
phrases.zh: 适合用途的；符合需要的
phrases.context: Warsh used the idea as part of his motto for making sure the Fed is suited to the challenges ahead.
phrases.example: The legacy ERP is no longer fit for purpose for a company operating in twelve markets.

phrases.meaning: a period that is neither very strong nor very weak economically
phrases.zh: 不温不火；既不繁荣也不萧条
phrases.context: He recalled the Bay Area of the late 1980s as a calm period between tech cycles.
phrases.example: The market is neither boom nor bust right now, which is a good window to negotiate long-term supplier contracts.

phrases.meaning: people or groups who behave dishonestly or try to cause harm
phrases.context: Warsh named the possibility of the technology being misused by harmful players as one of the risks.
phrases.example: Tighter onboarding checks will keep bad actors off the platform without slowing down legitimate sellers.
